topic: the four ways to exercise the mind
prompt: What four ways does the passage give for exercising the mind for mental excellence?

options.text: Research, meditation, the services of consultants, and insight-expectant prayer
Learning, understanding, reasoning and imagination
Quietness, separation, wise company and worship
Reading, writing, teaching and preaching

explanation: Four headings in the chapter, and the closing paragraph names them together: fact-finding adventures, meditation, engaging the services of consultants, and insight-expectant prayer.

why.a: Correct. These are the four, each with its own section.
why.b: Wrong. Those are the four FUNCTIONS of the mind, from Chapter 2. The book has several fours and they get confused.
why.c: Wrong. Quietness, separation and wise company are the three factors of the right ATMOSPHERE, from Chapter 7.
why.d: Wrong. None of these four are section headings anywhere in the book.

prompt: What questions did Isaac Newton ask when an apple dropped on his head?

options.text: Why did this thing fall? Why did it not stop in mid-air? What was pulling it?
What is the weight of this fruit, and what is the height of this tree?
Who sent this to me, and what does it mean?
How fast did it travel, and how far will it roll?

explanation: Three questions, and the third one, about what was pulling it, is what leads to gravity. He is offered as the model of exercising the mind, because he turned an ordinary event into a question.

why.a: Correct. These three questions are given in order, and they end at the force.
why.b: Wrong. Measurement is not what the story turns on.
why.c: Wrong. This makes it a providential sign rather than a scientific question, which is not how the book tells it.
why.d: Wrong. Speed and distance are not what he asked.

prompt: How does the passage describe research?

options.text: Engaging in fact-finding study: search, and if you can't find it, re-search, because it is there
Reading widely across many subjects for pleasure
Testing what you have been taught against experience
Collecting the opinions of experts on a question

explanation: The pun on re-search carries the definition, and the confidence behind it is that what you seek IS there, so failure means searching again rather than giving up.

why.a: Correct. Fact-finding study, with the re-search pun as its method.
why.b: Wrong. The book explicitly warns against reading for pleasure: many read for pleasure, no wonder they constantly live under pressure.
why.c: Wrong. Testing against experience is not the definition offered.
why.d: Wrong. Collecting expert opinion is CONSULTANTS, the third way, which is a separate section.

topic: the gift is only a seed
prompt: What does the passage say about the mind of Christ as a gift?

options.text: It is only a seed, which must be nurtured until it begins to bring forth fruits
It is complete at new birth and needs no development
It is given in measure according to a person's faith
It is withdrawn from those who do not use it

explanation: The seed image governs the chapter. Daniel is the proof: God gave him knowledge and skill in all learning, yet he still said 'I Daniel understood by books', because the gift alone could not handle it and the books had to help the gift.

why.a: Correct. A seed to be nurtured to fruit, which is why exercising the mind is necessary at all.
why.b: Wrong. This would make the whole chapter unnecessary.
why.c: Wrong. Measure according to faith is a Pauline idea from elsewhere that this book does not use.
why.d: Wrong. Wisdom CAN be lost in Chapter 5, but through changing your God and through pride, not simply through disuse of the gift.

prompt: How does the passage apply Proverbs 27:17, "iron sharpeneth iron"?

options.text: When you are searching or studying you are rubbing your ordinary mind with greater minds, and your dull mind is sharpened
Believers sharpen one another through mutual correction
Hardship sharpens a man more than comfort does
Debate is the best way to test an idea

explanation: The sharpening happens through study rather than through personal encounter, which is why the verse sits under RESEARCH. It matches Chapter 7's claim that reading is keeping company with the author.

why.a: Correct. Study rubs your mind against greater minds, and that is the sharpening.
why.b: Wrong. Mutual correction is the usual application of this verse, and it is not the one made here.
why.c: Wrong. Hardship is not the sharpening agent in this book.
why.d: Wrong. Debate is never discussed.

prompt: What does the passage say determines how colourful you will become mentally?

options.text: How studious you are, no matter how gifted you are
How gifted you are, no matter how studious
How early you began to learn
How many teachers you have had

explanation: 'No matter how gifted you are, how studious you are is what determines how colourful you will become mentally.' The gift is not enough, and the book says this is where many Christians miss it.

why.a: Correct. Studiousness is the variable, and the gift is explicitly subordinated to it here.
why.b: Wrong. This inverts the sentence, which grants the gift and then makes study decisive.
why.c: Wrong. Chapter 2 says age is not what determines old age, and Chapter 6 says inspiration has nothing to do with age.
why.d: Wrong. Teachers are not counted anywhere; David even claims more understanding than all his teachers.

prompt: What two things does the passage say about Paul under research?

options.text: He was a bookworm, and he always had a notebook by him rather than reading merely for pleasure
He read only the scriptures and nothing else
He gave up reading once his letters were written
He preferred hearing teachers to reading books

explanation: Cited to 1 Timothy 4:13 for the bookworm and 2 Timothy 4:13 for the notebook, which is the parchments verse from Chapter 2. Paul is called one of the most gifted men in the New Testament, which is why the example works.

why.a: Correct. Both claims are made, with a citation for each.
why.b: Wrong. The parchments were his own notes, and he asked for books as well.
why.c: Wrong. Chapter 2 makes the opposite point, that having written half the New Testament he was still carrying books about.
why.d: Wrong. No preference for hearing over reading is expressed.

prompt: What did the author do when told his briefcase had been left in the car as he was boarding a plane?

options.text: He stopped and said he was not going anywhere without it, unable to imagine a week away from his personal study notes
He sent someone to fetch it and delayed the flight
He continued the journey and bought new materials on arrival
He asked for it to be sent on after him

explanation: It is offered as evidence of a studious life, alongside Paul's parchments. The point is the refusal, not the inconvenience.

why.a: Correct. He refused to travel without it, because of the study notes inside.
why.b: Wrong. Delaying a flight is not what the passage says; he says he was not going.
why.c: Wrong. Replacing them is not the point, since the notes were personal.
why.d: Wrong. Sending it on would have left him a week without it, which is exactly what he could not imagine.

topic: read for pleasure live under pressure
prompt: What does the passage say about those who read for pleasure?

options.text: Many read for pleasure, no wonder they constantly live under pressure; it is time to study for insight
Reading for pleasure is a good beginning that leads to deeper study
Reading for pleasure is harmless if balanced with prayer
Reading for pleasure is the mark of a restful mind

explanation: The rhyme is the hook: pleasure and pressure. He adds that you should not read merely for religious satisfaction or as a routine morning devotion time either.

why.a: Correct. Pleasure against pressure, with study for insight as the alternative.
why.b: Wrong. It is presented as a fault rather than a stage.
why.c: Wrong. The book links it directly to living under pressure.
why.d: Wrong. Pressure, not rest, is what the passage attaches to it.

prompt: What does the passage say about committed readers, and how is a leader defined?

options.text: Every committed reader is a potential leader, and a leader is someone who sees ahead, beyond what others see, and knows a little better
Every leader must first have been taught by another leader
A leader is someone others are willing to follow
A leader is someone who can explain what he knows

explanation: The definition is knowledge-based, and the consequence follows: because he has what others need, they keep coming to him in search of it. It matches Anthony Robbins, whose teachers began consulting him.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are given, and the reader-to-leader line is repeated later in the chapter.
why.b: Wrong. Chapter 7 says you can make authors your friends in absentia, so no direct lineage is required.
why.c: Wrong. Willingness to follow is not how the book defines it; seeing ahead is.
why.d: Wrong. Explanation is not the criterion offered.

prompt: What nickname does the author give Anthony Robbins?

options.text: The 700-in-one man
The man of solutions
The instant celebrity
The consultant to presidents

explanation: The 700-in-one man, from the 700 books he read in high school. The other three options are all true descriptions of him from Chapter 2, but only this is the nickname.

why.a: Correct. This is the coined nickname, and it fixes the figure of 700.
why.b: Wrong. He BECAME a man of solutions in his school, which is a description rather than the nickname.
why.c: Wrong. He became an instant celebrity on finishing high school, also a description.
why.d: Wrong. He is a consultant to IBM and Presidents, again true but not the nickname.

prompt: What does David Yonggi Cho say his wife does every week?

options.text: She piles up the books she thinks he should read by his bedside, saying he would offend her if he did not read them
She reads to him from the scriptures each morning
She keeps his study free of interruptions
She summarises the books she has read for him

explanation: She told him she was not forcing him to read them, but that he would offend her if he did not, which is the detail that makes the story memorable.

why.a: Correct. Books by the bedside, with the gentle compulsion she describes.
why.b: Wrong. Reading aloud is not part of the story.
why.c: Wrong. Protecting his study is closer to Chapter 7's separation than to this anecdote.
why.d: Wrong. Summarising is not mentioned; the point is that HE reads them.

prompt: What does the passage say about David Yonggi Cho's congregation and his years in ministry?

options.text: He pastors the largest congregation on the earth and has been at it for about 40 years, and the fire is still burning
He pastors the largest congregation in Asia and has served 64 years
He founded several congregations over 72 years
He pastors the fastest growing congregation and has served 20 years

explanation: Largest congregation on the earth, about 40 years. Chapter 8 also calls him the pastor of the largest church in the world when naming him the ideal consultant on church growth.

why.a: Correct. Largest on earth, about forty years, fire still burning.
why.b: Wrong. Sixty-four years belongs to the unnamed minister later in the same chapter.
why.c: Wrong. Seventy-two years is Norman Vincent Pearle's ordained ministry, from Chapter 2.
why.d: Wrong. Twenty years is the span of the ministry structure planned in Chapter 2.

prompt: When asked whether he crams scriptures, what did the author reply?

options.text: "No, I don't, I eat them!"
"Only the ones I preach from"
"I read and think"
"I write them out until they stick"

explanation: He explains it: there are some scriptures he has read over and over again, so how will it not stick? Eating is the opposite of cramming, which is why the answer is memorable.

why.a: Correct. Eating rather than cramming is the reply as printed.
why.b: Wrong. No such qualification is made.
why.c: Wrong, and it is the closest trap. 'I read and think' is a real answer of his, but to a different question, about what he does with his time, in Chapter 1.
why.d: Wrong. Writing them out is not mentioned.

prompt: What does the passage say happens the more you read?

options.text: The more you discover that you don't know, and you find something new in a passage you have read for 20 years
The faster you are able to read
The less you need to consult others
The more confident you become in your own judgment

explanation: 1 Corinthians 8:2 is quoted alongside it: 'if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.' The instruction is: do not assume knowledge, consciously acquire it.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are in the passage, including the specific span of 20 years.
why.b: Wrong. Reading speed is never discussed.
why.c: Wrong. Consultants are the third way to exercise the mind, so the need for others increases rather than shrinks.
why.d: Wrong. The passage says the opposite: sit up, you don't know anything yet.

prompt: In the testimony given in this chapter, what broke up the woman's marriage and what book did she read?

options.text: Her stealing habit, and she read Dynamics Of Holiness after Bishop Abioye recommended it
Her husband's unbelief, and she read Towards Mental Exploits
Her stealing habit, and she read Towards Excellence in Life & Ministry
Her lying habit, and she read Signposts On The Road to Success

explanation: Married nine years, marriage broken by stealing, the habit dating from childhood. Bishop Abioye recommended Dynamics Of Holiness in the month of Visitation, and she has three children. The testimony is signed E.A.O. (Mrs.).

why.a: Correct. Stealing, and Dynamics Of Holiness on Bishop Abioye's recommendation.
why.b: Wrong. Unbelief is not the cause, and this book is not the one she read.
why.c: Wrong. The habit is right but Towards Excellence in Life & Ministry is a different book of the author's, cited in Chapter 9.
why.d: Wrong. Signposts On The Road to Success is E. W. Kenyon's book, quoted at the end of this chapter.

prompt: Whose greatest companion does the passage say meditation was?

options.text: Solomon, the wisest man in Bible history
David, who meditated day and night
Daniel, who understood by books
Isaac, who went out to meditate in the evening

explanation: Ecclesiastes 1:13-17 is quoted, where Solomon gave his heart to seek and search out by wisdom, and communed with his own heart. He is said to have been addicted to the art of meditation.

why.a: Correct. Solomon, and the book calls meditation the secret behind his mental fertility.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the strongest trap, because David IS the meditation example in Chapter 2, from Psalm 119.
why.c: Wrong. Daniel is the research and prayer example in this chapter.
why.d: Wrong. Isaac's meditation is genuinely in the book, but in Chapter 7 under separation.

prompt: What does the author think is the missing asset in the Church today?

options.text: Meditation
Reading
Prayer
Counsel

explanation: 'I think meditation is the missing asset in the Church today.' The reason: so many are given to rigorous reading and studies, but very few take time to ponder the facts and issues involved.

why.a: Correct. Meditation is named, and the diagnosis is that reading happens without pondering.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the trap, because the passage explicitly grants that reading IS happening rigorously. Pondering is what is missing.
why.c: Wrong. Chapter 2 does say the Church has long lost the art of thinking, but the missing asset named here is meditation.
why.d: Wrong. Counsel is the third way in this chapter but is not called the missing asset.

prompt: What questions does the passage tell you to ask in meditation?

options.text: What could be responsible for this? Why is it like this? Can't it be otherwise?
What does this mean for me? What must I now do?
Who wrote this, and what did they intend?
Is this true, and can it be proved?

explanation: Causal and counterfactual questions. If you have read and not assimilated much, you are told to settle down, ponder, and start grinding it mentally, believing there must be a solution.

why.a: Correct. These three are the questions given, and the last one is the creative turn.
why.b: Wrong, and it is close, because Chapter 2's questions for processing knowledge into understanding do run this way. But these are the meditation questions in Chapter 8.
why.c: Wrong. Authorial intent is never a question the book raises.
why.d: Wrong. Verification is not the aim of meditation here.

prompt: What does the passage say about Moses and Jethro?

options.text: Moses would have died under a heavy load of responsibility but for the counsel of Jethro, his father-in-law
Jethro taught Moses the law before Sinai
Jethro warned Moses not to return to Egypt
Moses appointed Jethro as a judge over Israel

explanation: Jethro is one of two counsellor examples in this section, with Ahitophel. The author adds that Jethro's godly counsel, he believes, helped Moses to live long.

why.a: Correct. The heavy load of responsibility and Jethro's counsel are both named.
why.b: Wrong. Teaching the law is not part of this account.
why.c: Wrong. The return to Egypt is not mentioned in this book.
why.d: Wrong. It was Jethro who advised appointing judges; the book does not go into that detail.

prompt: How does the passage describe Ahitophel's role and the weight of his counsel?

options.text: He was the think-tank of David's government, and his counsel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God
He was David's chief priest, and his counsel was law
He was a prophet whose words always came to pass
He was a scribe who kept the records of the kingdom

explanation: 2 Samuel 16:23 is quoted, and it notes that this held true both with David and with Absalom. He later went with Absalom when he rebelled against his father.

why.a: Correct. Think-tank is the author's word, and the oracle comparison is the verse's own.
why.b: Wrong. He was a counsellor, not a priest.
why.c: Wrong. Prophecy is not his described office.
why.d: Wrong. Record keeping is never mentioned.

prompt: Who is quoted saying "If I have seen any farther, it is because I am standing on the shoulders of those who have gone before me"?

options.text: Isaac Newton
Abraham Lincoln
Zig Ziglar
E. W. Kenyon

explanation: Isaac Newton, who appears twice in this chapter: once for the apple and the law of gravity, and again here under consultants.

why.a: Correct. Newton is quoted for both the apple and the shoulders.
why.b: Wrong. Lincoln's lines are about learning and age, in Chapters 2 and 8.
why.c: Wrong. Zig Ziglar's line is about imagination being the most powerful nation, in Chapter 2.
why.d: Wrong. Kenyon's line about making your brain work closes this chapter.

prompt: What does the passage say it takes to enjoy the ministry of counsellors?

options.text: Meekness, because a proud-hearted man will always have reasons why the counsel will not work in his case
Money, because good counsel is never free
Time, because counsel must be tested slowly
Discernment, because much counsel is false

explanation: The proud man's excuses are named: he will say the consultant is only lucky, or that he has some advantage. Meekness is also the third requirement for divine wisdom in Chapter 4, so the theme carries.

why.a: Correct. Meekness, with the proud man's characteristic excuses spelled out.
why.b: Wrong. Cost is never mentioned; consultants often come through books and tapes.
why.c: Wrong. Delay is not counselled.
why.d: Wrong. The test given elsewhere is whether it is profiting the person, not suspicion of falsehood.

prompt: Which two visits does the author credit with changing his perspective on how to run an office and a ministry?

options.text: Dr. Frederick K. C. Price's office and the Oral Roberts University
Kenneth E. Hagin's office in Tulsa and David Yonggi Cho's church
Archbishop Benson Idahosa's ministry in Benin and a church in Accra
T. L. Osborn's headquarters and Bishop Abioye's church

explanation: At Price's office his perspective changed on what an office environment should be; at Oral Roberts University he saw the classic business perspective and said 'It can be done anywhere.'

why.a: Correct. These two visits are the ones credited here.
why.b: Wrong. He did visit Hagin in Tulsa, but that is in Chapter 2 and is about finding him READING. Cho is cited through his books, not a visit.
why.c: Wrong. Idahosa appears in Chapter 10 pointing at a building, and Accra was a solitary trip in Chapter 7.
why.d: Wrong. Osborn is quoted but never visited, and Abioye appears only in the testimony.

prompt: Whom did Daniel involve when the king demanded the dream and its interpretation?

options.text: Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, his companions
The queen and the king's counsellors
The other wise men of Babylon
No one; he prayed alone

explanation: He asked them to desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret, so that Daniel and his fellows should not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Then the secret was revealed in a night vision.

why.a: Correct. His three companions are named, by their Hebrew names.
why.b: Wrong. The queen belongs to the OTHER Daniel story, at Belshazzar's feast.
why.c: Wrong. The other wise men were the ones in danger, not partners in prayer.
why.d: Wrong. The passage names three companions, which is part of why it is quotable.

prompt: How does the passage paraphrase Daniel's insight-expectant prayer?

options.text: "Lord, I don't know it, but I know You know it. God of heaven, show it now"
"Lord, give me the wisdom I lack, and upbraid me not"
"Lord, deliver us from the king's decree"
"Lord, remember Your covenant with our fathers"

explanation: The instruction that follows is the point: pray insight-expectant prayers, not just blank prayers. The prayer names what is wanted, which is what makes it insight-expectant.

why.a: Correct. This is the paraphrase as given, and it asks for the specific thing.
why.b: Wrong. That is the sense of James 1:5, which IS cited nearby, but it is not this paraphrase.
why.c: Wrong. Deliverance from the decree is the situation rather than the prayer's content.
why.d: Wrong. Covenant language is not used in this prayer.

prompt: What happened when the author locked himself in his office over his little daughter?

options.text: Under one hour, three powerful scriptures with fire in them came alive in his spirit
He prayed for three days before an answer came
He received a night vision as Daniel did
He called for other ministers to join him

explanation: Under one hour, three scriptures, and with them the sting of death was banished, death was swallowed up in victory, and Jesus was glorified.

why.a: Correct. Under one hour and three scriptures are the two figures given.
why.b: Wrong. Three days belongs to the prosperity trip in Chapter 7.
why.c: Wrong. The book explicitly says you do NOT have to sleep like Daniel waiting for a night vision, because the more awake you are the more mentally alert you become.
why.d: Wrong. He locked the doors, which is the opposite of calling others in.

prompt: Who wrote "Signposts On The Road to Success", and what is quoted from it?

options.text: E. W. Kenyon: "Make your brain work; it will sweat, but make it work"
David Oyedepo: "Make your brain work; it will sweat, but make it work"
E. W. Kenyon: "When you stop learning, you start dying"
Kenneth E. Hagin: "Make your brain work; it will sweat, but make it work"

explanation: The quotation continues: then it will improve, it will develop, until you become the envy of those around you. The chapter's conclusion is that you have to make it work before it begins to work for you.

why.a: Correct. Kenyon wrote the book and this is the line quoted from it.
why.b: Wrong. The author's own books named in this text are Dynamics Of Holiness and Towards Excellence in Life & Ministry.
why.c: Wrong. That line is T. L. Osborn's, quoted in Chapters 2 and 8.
why.d: Wrong. Hagin appears for the T. L. Osborn book on his table and the 1996 healing book.

prompt: What does the passage say about putting your mind to work and God?

options.text: Until you put your mind to work, God will not mind you, and it is the exercise of the mind that produces excellence
God works whether or not you engage your mind
God rewards the willing heart above the working mind
God supplies the mind's work when you rest in Him

explanation: It reprises Chapter 1's pun, where it is the use to which you put your mind that makes the world MIND you. Here the same wordplay is applied to God.

why.a: Correct. Both halves are stated, and the pun on mind is deliberate.
why.b: Wrong. This contradicts the chapter's demand for conscious participation.
why.c: Wrong. Willingness is a condition in Isaiah 1:19 but is never set above mental work.
why.d: Wrong. Chapter 2 says plainly that God will not think for you.

prompt: Which proverb is quoted as "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety"?

options.text: Proverbs 11:14
Proverbs 15:22
Proverbs 20:18
Proverbs 19:20

explanation: Four counsel proverbs are quoted in a row here, and they are easy to confuse. 11:14 has safety, 15:22 has purposes established, 19:20-21 has wise in thy latter end, and 20:18 has make war with good advice.

why.a: Correct. Proverbs 11:14 is the safety verse.
why.b: Wrong. Proverbs 15:22 is 'Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.'
why.c: Wrong. Proverbs 20:18 is 'Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.'
why.d: Wrong. Proverbs 19:20 is 'Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.'

prompt: What does the author say he would do on seeing someone who has stayed on successfully in ministry for 64 years?

options.text: Learn from him how to keep alive and still be productive in old age, and write to him if he needs extra knowledge
Invite him to speak to his congregation
Record his story before it is lost
Encourage him to hand over to a successor

explanation: It grows out of Psalm 92:14, that even in old age they shall still bring forth fruit. He says he wants productive longevity, not just to be alive but alive serving God.

why.a: Correct. Learning from him, and writing a letter asking him to explain something, are both mentioned.
why.b: Wrong. Invitations are not part of this passage.
why.c: Wrong. Recording histories is never discussed.
why.d: Wrong. Succession is not raised; the point is continued productivity.

prompt: Fill the blank: "Every committed reader is a potential {{1}}."
explanation: Leader, and the rhyme with reader is why it sticks. The book repeats the line later in the same chapter when charging Timothy to give attention to reading.

prompt: The passage says you must sleep, as Daniel did, and wait for insight to be revealed in a night vision.

options.text: True
False

explanation: False. 'You don't have to sleep like Daniel, waiting for it to be revealed in a night vision. In fact, the more awake you are, the more conscious and mentally alert you become.'

why.true: Wrong. Daniel's night vision is reported, but the book explicitly says you do not have to follow that route.
why.false: Correct. Wakefulness is preferred, because alertness is what the book is after throughout.

prompt: What does the passage say the evidence of your studies must be?

options.text: Freedom from sickness, sin, sorrow and suffering, joy oozing forth, and great results from your work
The number of books you have finished
The respect of those who teach you
The ability to answer any question put to you

explanation: Four s-words plus visible joy and results. The demand is that study show itself in life, not in accumulation, which is why reading merely for religious satisfaction is rejected.

why.a: Correct. All of these are named as the evidence that you are really devoted in your search and studies.
why.b: Wrong. Counting books is closer to the local champion's small yardstick than to this test.
why.c: Wrong. Respect from teachers happened to Anthony Robbins, but it is not the test set here.
why.d: Wrong. Answers are a product of divine wisdom in Chapter 5, not the evidence of study.
